idiom_name: pure functions over const-correct structs + a thin IO translation unit
implementation_notes: Nothing in C enforces purity, so the split is hand-written discipline: the core is a translation unit of functions that take their inputs as values or `const T *`, touch no globals, allocate nothing, and return the result by value (`typedef struct { ... } Quote;`), while the shell is the file that calls `fopen`/`read`/`write`, builds the input struct out of what it read, calls one core function and carries out the returned decision. Mark read-only pointer parameters `const` (CERT DCL13-C) so the compiler diagnoses writes through them, and keep the core free of stdio, time, rand and malloc - that import/`#include` list is the audit trail, since the compiler cannot see an effect. The classic structure of function-pointer 'ports' is only worth writing where the core must call back into the world, which is exactly what the pattern removes; a struct plus a status code covers the normal case.
pitfalls: `const T *` stops writes through that pointer, but the caller can still reach the same object through another path and mutate it while the 'pure' function is running (aliasing); if the core keeps or returns a pointer into its input, the value it decided on may change afterwards.

Struct copies are shallow: a struct holding a `char *` or an array member shares the pointed-to buffer with the shell, so passing by value is isolation only when the core owns a copy or the buffer stays `const` for the whole call.

Nothing checks the boundary: a stray `time(NULL)`, `rand()` or `getenv()` inside the core compiles, links and passes review; purity survives only through review plus a CI gate on the core's includes, and a core that allocates forces the shell to know who frees what.
